AI-Based Automated Evaluation of Handwritten
Descriptive Answer Scripts Using Vision-Language
OCR and Constraint-Aware LLM Grading

Abstract—Evaluation of handwritten descriptive answer scripts
has always been considered difficult due to handwriting differ-
ences, OCR errors, semantics variability of students’ answers,
and specific rules for grading in the particular examination pro-
cess. The existing approaches to automated assessments mainly
involve using the clean digital version of text and lexical matching
techniques, restricting their application in real-life scenarios
of handwritten examinations. This paper proposes an end-to-
end AI-powered system that combines Vision-Language Optical
Character Recognition (OCR) and constraint-aware Large Lan-
guage Model (LLM) in order to provide semantic grading of
handwritten answer scripts.

A Florence-2 vision-language model
that was fine-tuned on the IAM Handwriting Database is used
for recognizing handwritten texts in a reliable way followed
by an answer alignment algorithm that aligns the answers to
questions considering the peculiarities of the examination process
structure. The grading is performed by locally running Llama
3 (8B) grading engine that evaluates the answers according to
the grading rubrics, including the marking scheme, optional
questions, and section-wise grading. Index Terms—Automated Essay Scoring (AES), Handwritten
Text Recognition, Vision-Language Models, Florence-2, Large
Language Models, Semantic Answer Assessment, Constraint-
Aware Grading, Educational AI. I. INTRODUCTION
Descriptive tests through handwriting still form one of the
main methods of evaluating the students’ conceptual knowl-
edge, analytical skills, and problem-solving skills in education
centers. Nonetheless, manual assessment of such handwritten
answer papers involves intensive work, delays, and is always
subjective, leading to inconsistent scoring and late posting
of the results. As the number of students keeps increasing,
there is an increased need for intelligent automated systems
for conducting assessments [1], [14], [16]. The latest developments in NLP, VLMs, and LLMs have
greatly enhanced Automated Essay Scoring and document
understanding [5], [10], [18]. However, most AES tools are
designed for digitally typed texts or make use of lexical
matching and thus do not apply to handwritten descriptive
exams where variations in handwriting styles, OCR mistakes,
and different ways of writing an answer continue to be a
problem [1], [9], [13].

In addition, existing methods hardly
combine handwritten text recognition with semantic grading
and take into account examination-specific marking criteria. In order to overcome such shortcomings, this paper presents
an end-to-end AI-based framework that integrates a Florence-2
Vision-Language OCR model with a constraint-aware Llama 3
(8B) grading engine for automated evaluation of handwritten
descriptive answers. In this way, Florence-2 will be trained
on the IAM Handwriting Database in order to increase the
performance of OCR of handwritten text regardless of the
diversity in writing style and conditions of documents. Au-
tomatically aligned responses will be semantically evaluated
against predefined answers set by instructors. Grading will
also take into account examination-related constraints such as
marking schemes and section-wise allocation of marks. The major contributions of this work are summarized as
follows:
• An end-to-end framework integrating Florence-2 Vision-
Language OCR with a constraint-aware Llama 3 grading
engine for handwritten descriptive answer evaluation.
• An automated answer-alignment mechanism capable of
handling complex examination layouts and optional-
question structures.
• A rubric-guided semantic grading strategy that combines
contextual reasoning with examination-specific grading
constraints.
• Experimental
evaluation
on
the
IAM
Handwriting
Database and a curated handwritten examination dataset,

demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed frame-
work for practical educational assessment. II. LITERATURE SURVEY
The automated evaluation of handwritten descriptive an-
swer scripts is an important research topic that lies at the
intersection of computer vision, natural language processing,
and educational technology. In earlier Automated Essay Scor-
ing (AES) systems, the use of lexical features and manu-
ally crafted rules was predominant which prevented them
from assessing semantic comprehension. Recent progress in
Vision-Language Models (VLMs), handwriting recognition,
and Large Language Models (LLMs) has made it possible
to improve document understanding and semantic evaluation
significantly. However, current techniques do not integrate
the tasks of handwriting recognition and answer evaluation,
taking into account examination specific constraints and rubric
based evaluation. This work tries to overcome this problem by
providing an integrated system for the end-to-end evaluation
of handwritten descriptive answer scripts. A. Automated Essay and Answer-Sheet Scoring with NLP and
LLMs
First-generation AES systems made use of lexical prop-
erties, rules designed by humans, and keyword matching
for mimicking human evaluation [1], [14]. While efficient
from the computational point of view, these methods did not
have the capacity to incorporate semantic comprehension and
conceptual accuracy [13]. Syntactic and linguistic features
used in machine learning algorithms enhanced consistency of
scoring yet were task-specific and lacked generalizability [6],
[15], [18]. The introduction of Transformer-based language models has
greatly contributed to the automation of assessment via contex-
tual semantic reasoning.

Transformer-based AES models have
been shown to exhibit high agreement with human assessors
[4], [10], [12], and the recent use of LLaMA-based models
has facilitated rubric-driven assessment via semantic analysis
and explanation [2], [7], [8]. Nevertheless, existing grading systems based on LLMs
make use of digitized data [5], [16] and disregard problems
associated with handwriting. Errors in OCR adversely affect
subsequent analysis on the semantic level, thereby decreasing
the accuracy of grading. In spite of the fact that some recent
works have considered multi-modal handwritten answer sheet
assessment [20], Vision-Language OCR with constraint-aware
LLM grading has not been sufficiently studied yet. B. Vision-Language Models for Handwritten Document Un-
derstanding
Automated comprehension of handwritten documents still
continues to be a key problem in automated educational assess-
ment because of differences in handwriting, document quality,
and page layout complexity. Traditional HTR systems yielded
encouraging results on standard datasets such as the IAM
Handwriting Database [13], [18], although their effectiveness

dropped significantly in the case of handwritten examination
documents with noise text and drawings [16]. The emergence of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has led
to an increased efficiency in document understanding owing to
the combined modeling of visual and textual data.

In contrast
to the traditional OCR pipeline that separates these two types
of data, vision-language models such as Florence-2 are capable
of performing end-to-end text extraction through prompting
and are more robust to variations in handwriting and document
layout [20]. Even with all these advancements, current literature mainly
concentrates on handwriting recognition technology instead of
the use of these technologies in AI-based marking solutions. The presented approach seeks to fill this gap by merging the
Vision-Language OCR system with the constraint-aware LLM
grading approach. C. Research Gap
Current automated grading systems concentrate on either
one or the other of these two aspects, but hardly ever have
an integrated approach. Furthermore, constraint-based grading,
offline operation, and scalability in handwriting evaluation of
descriptive answers are not commonly supported [13], [16],
[18]. III. PROPOSED FRAMEWORK
In the proposed framework, an end-to-end framework of AI-
driven approach to automate the assessment of handwritten
descriptive answer scripts is proposed based on the combi-
nation of Vision-Language OCR, semantic reasoning using
Large Language Model (LLM), and asynchronous inference
management. Contrary to the traditional method where the
task of handwritten text recognition and answer assessment is
performed independently, the proposed framework creates an
end-to-end processing pipeline to convert handwritten exami-
nation documents to structured texts for semantic assessment. Evaluation is a multi-stage process that starts from scanning
of question papers and handwritten answer sheets in PDF
or image format.

Handwritten document understanding using
the Florence-2 Vision-Language OCR component involves
extraction of the textual content while keeping the context
and structure of the original document intact. Subsequently,
the extracted text goes through the Llama 3-based semantic
evaluation engine that evaluates the conceptual similarity of
the answers provided by the students to the answers given Fig. 1. Overall architecture of the proposed evaluation framework.
by the instructor. To facilitate the batch processing of a
high number of answer scripts, the asynchronous queue-based
inference mechanism is utilized for the orchestration of GPU-
intensive OCR and LLM computations, with the help of the
light-weight SQLite database storing all extracted text, results
of evaluation and metadata. A. Vision-Language OCR Module
The Vision-Language OCR module converts handwritten
examination papers into readable text format, which can be
analyzed semantically. The OCR module is not like regular
OCRs since it uses the Florence-2 Vision-Language Model
that has both visual and linguistic components to interpret
handwritten text. Given an input handwritten document,

The Constraint Aware LLM Grading Module uses semantic
evaluation where the student’s answer is matched with the
reference answer provided by the teacher. Unlike traditional
approaches of keyword matching for grading, the suggested
approach involves the use of Llama 3 for reasoning on the
conceptual semantics of the answer texts. Let the extracted student response and reference answer be
represented as

where C denotes the examination constraints and g(·)
represents the constraint-aware grading function. By jointly
considering semantic understanding and evaluation constraints,
the proposed module produces reliable and consistent grading
results for handwritten descriptive answer scripts. C. Asynchronous Inference and Data Management
Asynchronous Inference and Data Management is used to
ensure efficient functioning of the proposed solution while
ensuring that the evaluation data remains stored reliably. Due
to the computational resource needs of both Florence-2 Vision-
Language OCR model and Llama 3 semantic grading model,
processing multiple answer scripts at the same time may cause
the GPU resource conflicts. The solution to the problem is
the use of asynchronous queuing scheduling approach by the
proposed framework which will process answer scripts one by
one. Every uploaded answer script is queued for evaluation and
graded independently using the OCR module and semantic
grading module. This sequential scheduling avoids any conflict
in GPU inference, optimizes the usage of resources, and allows
the batch processing of handwritten answer scripts. Once the evaluation is completed, the output text, evaluation
outcomes, and metadata are stored in a SQLite database per-
manently.

This database acts as a centralized storage medium
for maintaining evaluation information. This helps in retrieving
the results easily, auditing them and performing any future
analysis on them. By combining asynchronous inference with
persistent storage, we propose an efficient approach to auto-
mated evaluation of handwritten answers. IV. DATASET AND IMPLEMENTATION
A. Dataset Preparation
The effectiveness of the developed Vision-Language OCR
module relies on the recognition of varied handwriting samples
encountered in the handwriting of handwritten exam papers. As a way of improving the recognition of handwritten texts,
IAM Handwriting Database has been chosen to be used as
the main training database since it has been extensively used
as the standard for HTR. In addition, multimodal document
understanding has recently been introduced as an essential
part of automatic assessment systems prompting the need to
develop a Vision-Language OCR system [20]. IAM database consists of over 1,500 scanned handwritten
pages by 657 different writers, including around 13,000 la-
beled text lines and above 115,000 word images. There is
a high variability in handwriting styles, character spacing,
strokes, and handwriting quality in this database which enables
learning strong visual representations for practical handwritten
documents. Before the training process, the handwriting samples along
with their ground truth transcriptions were prepared as image-
text pair data suitable for training with the Florence-2 system. Validation, preprocessing, and formatting of the data ensured
that the correlation between the handwritten data and the text
was maintained.

Such preparation helps the Vision-Language
model learn the mapping between the handwriting data and
its corresponding text, providing valid text data for automated
answer evaluation using AI [16], [20]. B. Florence-2 Fine-Tuning
Though the Florence-2 model is pretrained on the general
vision-language understanding task, its capability of recogniz-
ing handwritten texts from the unconstrained exam scripts is
constrained. In order to increase the recognition accuracy of
the model, it was fine-tuned through the IAM Handwriting
Database that had been prepared before [18], [20]. The training dataset consists of image-text pairs (I, T),
where I represents the handwritten image and T denotes its
corresponding ground-truth transcription. During fine-tuning,
the model learns the optimal parameters by minimizing the
OCR sequence prediction loss,

C. System Implementation
This framework was implemented in a modular and offline-
first design to guarantee a reliable and scalable evaluation
of handwritten descriptive answers scripts. The framework
incorporates three main modules: Vision-Language OCR, se-
mantic grading with constraints, and asynchronous inference
management [16], [20]. The backend was built with the use of Python and Flask,
coordinating the entire process from the preprocessing of the
documents to OCR detection, semantic analysis, and the man-
agement of the results using an execution pipeline. The model
used for handwritten text extraction is called Florence-2. The
local deployment of Llama 3, using Ollama, is responsible
for semantic analysis without the need for any cloud-based
services [19], [20]. The framework utilizes an asynchronous queue to schedule
OCR and LLM inference tasks separately to ensure no GPU
contention occurs during simultaneous operations. Results, text
output, and metadata are permanently stored in an efficient
and lightweight SQLite database for efficient retrieval, result
tracking, and management. This makes the design flexible
enough such that the different modules can work separately
but in a coherent manner to accommodate future incorporation
of other OCR and LLM models or grading techniques [16]. V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
A. OCR Performance Evaluation
The suggested module of Vision-Language OCR was tested
using the IAM Handwriting Database, a well-known dataset
used in handwritten text recognition studies.

As OCR quality
influences the quality of semantic grading, recognition quality
was examined in terms of handwriting style diversity and
implementation features [20]. The optimized Florence-2 system was benchmarked against
Tesseract OCR, CRNN-CTC, TrOCR Base, and Groq Vision
API based on Character Error Rate (CER), off-line operation,
and multimodal document understanding [16], [20]. The experimental results show that the suggested Florence-
2 model exhibits comparable OCR accuracy, with the capacity
to deploy in an offline setting and to process multimodal docu-
ments. This contrasts with traditional OCR systems that focus
on text recognition or cloud services that require connectivity,
and it offers a secure and private solution for evaluating hand-
written answers [13], [18], [20]. The quantitative comparison
of the evaluated OCR models is presented in Table II. Table II demonstrates that Florence-2 is a multimodal docu-
ment understanding system which, at the same time, provides
high recognition accuracy and offline operation. Although
Tesseract OCR, CRNN-CTC, and TrOCR Base offer offline
inference but not multimodality, Groq Vision API offers mul-
timodal reasoning but requires cloud connectivity. Thus, the
proposed Florence-2 system can be used effectively for offline
handwriting evaluation. B. Semantic Grading Performance
To test the semantic grading capabilities of the proposed
framework, experiments were carried out by comparing the
OCR-extracted answers of students with the answers provided
by the instructor with the help of Llama 3 grading module. Un-
like traditional methods which work on the basis of keyword
matching, language models conduct semantic evaluation by
evaluating the concepts instead of matching lexical forms [5],
[10], [18].

Thus, the proposed framework conducts conceptual
evaluation via semantic reasoning. Grading is conducted in an integrated way with respect
to the grading question, reference answer, and the student’s
answer, focusing on semantic similarity as opposed to lexical
similarity. This method increases robustness for paraphrased
answers, synonyms, and differences in arrangement usually
associated with descriptive tests [7], [9], [11]. As per the experimental outcomes, it is shown that the
suggested semantic grading system is very much in accordance
with the expectation of instructors with respect to consistency
in grading the handwritten answers. Moreover, inclusion of
fine-tuned Vision-Language OCR system helps avoid the er-
rors due to OCR in the subsequent semantic evaluations [16],
[19], [20]. C. Novelty
This solution solves all the shortcomings in the following
ways: through the use of a refined version of Florence-2
Vision-Language OCR model along with a grading engine of
Llama 3 with constraint awareness, asynchronous queue infer-
ence, and results management in SQLite database, providing
an offline-first design. VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this paper, we proposed an AI-Based Automated Evalu-
ation Framework for Handwritten Descriptive Answer Scripts
by leveraging a fine-tuned Florence-2 Vision-Language OCR
model and a constraint-aware Llama 3 semantic grading
engine. Our framework can automate the whole evaluation
process in terms of extracting handwritten text, conducting
semantic evaluation, managing asynchronous inference, and
storing results within an offline-first system. Experimental
evaluation proved that our fine-tuned Florence-2 model attains
comparable OCR accuracy while allowing for the seman-
tic grading capability via context reasoning.

Moreover, the
proposed approach is scalable, efficient in GPU usage, and
easily integrates OCR and LLM evaluation into educational
assessment. The future of our research will involve adapting the pro-
